profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in a hospital pharmacovigilance unit after a pilot method-selection worksheet, built from a systematic review of spontaneous reporting system signal detection methods, generated different recommendations for the same example safety scenarios during two internal dry runs. The team is preparing an internal memo for the medication safety committee on which ADR signal detection methods should be used in different reporting contexts, but the worksheet now appears unreliable when applied to FAERS extracts and the hospital’s local spontaneous reports. The agenda is to diagnose why the recommendations changed, determine whether the problem lies in the interpretation of the review factors or in the preprocessing workflow, and agree on a practical fix before the memo is finalized. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting plan for a 'stable' and defensible method-selection workflow for next week's committee packet.

members.name: Dr. Linh Tran
members.expertise: ADR case assessment, medication safety review, signal triage, interpretation of spontaneous reporting data
members.background: Dr. Tran leads the hospital’s drug safety surveillance group and previously served on a regional pharmacovigilance review panel; she routinely translates quantitative signal outputs into recommendations that can withstand clinician scrutiny, but she does not inspect the technical preprocessing scripts herself.
members.private_state: She wants the memo to look methodologically steady and credible to the medication safety committee, so that the committee does not reopen the broader question of how the unit chooses signal detection methods. She is especially worried about missing early, clinically serious signals for newer oncology and immunology products.
hidden_assumptions: When a method is described as 'better-performing,' it means it is more useful for expert review because it surfaces clinically plausible and consequential signals early, even if the output is sparse.

The 'database' relevant to choosing a method is the operational reporting pool currently under review, so local hospital reports and a FAERS extract are separate decision contexts rather than one combined analytic environment.
A 'stable' workflow is one whose recommendations look consistent enough across similar safety scenarios that the memo remains credible and does not appear arbitrary to the committee.
Routine duplicate cleaning should already collapse all same-case repeat and follow-up submissions into one clinically sensible case record before any method comparison is interpreted.

The analyst's standard preprocessing script probably follows ordinary pharmacovigilance case logic, so there is no reason to inspect its duplicate-handling details unless something is obviously broken.

members.name: Mei Chen
members.expertise: Spontaneous reporting system analytics, disproportionality algorithms, Bayesian shrinkage methods, reproducible review pipelines
members.background: Chen built the pilot method-selection worksheet that maps review scenarios to candidate signal detection methods and previously validated FAERS-based signal screening workflows in an academic drug safety lab; she relies on documented preprocessing conventions and version-controlled scripts rather than manual case-by-case curation.
members.private_state: She wants to show that the worksheet logic is fundamentally sound and that the recommendation shifts mostly reflect data handling and rerun reproducibility, not a flaw in the overall framework. She also wants to avoid a last-minute redesign before the committee deadline.
hidden_assumptions: When a method is 'better-performing,' it means it behaves more robustly under fixed analytic conditions, such as producing reproducible rankings or thresholds across reruns and resampled subsets.

The 'database size' factor from the review refers to the effective standardized analytic dataset available to the method after pooling compatible reports, not the organizational source where reports originated.

A 'stable' workflow is one whose outputs are reproducible at the code and ranking level under the same specification; if scores move materially between reruns, the workflow is not yet stable even if the narrative recommendation sounds similar.

The existing FAERS-style preprocessing script removes exact duplicate case records but keeps medically informative follow-up versions unless they are literal repeats, and that convention is standard enough not to require discussion.

Because the duplicate-handling script is the inherited standard script from her prior lab and has been running without errors, nontechnical collaborators generally assume its cleaning rules match the intended preprocessing logic.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss choosing the 'better-performing' or 'best-performing' signal detection method for a given safety scenario.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a method that is more clinically useful for triage: it should bring forward plausible, serious ADR signals early enough for expert review, even if it flags fewer pairs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a method that is technically more robust: it should produce more reproducible signal behavior under fixed preprocessing and reruns, with less sensitivity to small input changes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a troubleshooting meeting, 'better-performing' sounds like an obviously shared evaluative term, and both interpretations are professionally legitimate; because neither is arguing against performance, the differing criteria stay beneath the surface.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to method choice depending on whether the 'database' is small or large.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is classifying each reporting stream as its own decision context, so the hospital's local spontaneous reports count as a small database and the current FAERS pull is a separate larger database.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the pooled standardized analytic file used in the worksheet, which combines compatible local and FAERS reports for tuning and testing and therefore counts as large enough for shrinkage-based methods.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'database size' is lifted directly from the systematic review language, so both assume they are invoking the same factor; the hidden difference is the unnoticed boundary around what belongs to the database in the first place.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the method-selection workflow needs to be 'stable' before the committee sees it.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the workflow should look consistent and defensible in the memo: comparable clinical scenarios should not suddenly receive different method-family recommendations in a way that undermines the memo's credibility.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the workflow should be reproducible at the implementation level: rerunning the same specification should yield similar scores, rankings, and worksheet outputs from the code.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because 'stability' is an expected troubleshooting goal, each hears the other's use of the word as support for her own concern; the surface agreement is reinforced by the fact that reproducible code and credible recommendations often correlate, though they are not the same thing.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'clean the duplicates first'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that they should 'clean the duplicates first' before rerunning the method-selection examples.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes duplicate cleaning means collapsing repeat submissions and all linked follow-up versions for the same case into one clinically curated case representation before comparing methods.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes duplicate cleaning means rerunning the inherited standard script, which removes exact duplicate records but preserves nonidentical follow-up reports that update seriousness, outcome, or narrative fields.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Duplicate cleaning sounds like mundane preprocessing rather than a substantive methodological choice, and M1 has never reviewed the inherited script itself; meanwhile M2 assumes that saying 'standard script' implicitly resolves the details, so neither realizes they are imagining different procedures.
